content.thinking:
I'm planning the full character build in one pass, designing a humanoid support-medic skeleton with hips, spine, chest, head, articulated arms and legs, plus a healing staff held in the right hand.

I'm settling on a palette: off-white and mid-grey armor plating over dark graphite undersuit, with a strong teal-cyan accent glow for the healing effect, warm skin tone for the human side of the face, and metallic tones for the cyborg side. Since there's no typechecking available, I'll be deliberate about only importing what I actually use and mapping out the full coordinate skeleton before writing any code.

Now I'm figuring out the joint hierarchy — setting hip height around 1.85m total with Overwatch-style heroic proportions, planning a spine chain from hips to chest using a catmull curve with careful attention to matching knot counts to joint names so I don't accidentally create an extra tip joint. I'm deciding to simplify the torso construction by attaching rigid parts directly to bones rather than building sweeps along chains, since that's more reliable for this kind of armored build.

For the actual torso skin, I'm planning a smooth sweep along the spine chain to form the undersuit body, with rigid armor plates layered on top — fitting since Overwatch-style characters favor plate armor over continuous skin deformation. I'm working out the radius function for the sweep, tapering the waist narrower than the chest, and extending the chain up toward the neck base for a clean transition.

Now I'm setting the spine chain's control points up from hip to chest height, naming the joints spine1, spine2, and chest, with the neck and arms parented off the chest joint. For the pelvis, I'm sweeping a short rigid section between hip points using an elliptical cross-section rigged to the hips bone, then planning the leg limbs running from hip joints down to the ankles.

For the toe joint, I'm weighing role options like "digit" versus "hinge" since it sits at the tip of the foot chain, aiming the ankle's end tangent downward into the foot.

For the limb, I'm treating the chain as a polyline of points from hip to ankle and sweeping a tube over it with a varying radius function -- thicker at the thigh, tapering at the knee, bulging slightly for the calf, then narrowing at the ankle, using a small keyed array of radius values spaced across the path.

Over that bare tube I'll layer armor plates rigidly attached to the bones using frustumBox shapes between joint points, with width along the binormal and height along the forward normal so the plates orient correctly down the leg. For the arms, I'm setting up shoulder joints parented to the chest at symmetric offsets and will build the arm segments similarly.

Now I'm working out the A-pose joint positions for the arms—computing elbow and wrist coordinates from shoulder using trig with a roughly 25° outward angle and specific upper/forearm lengths, adding a slight forward bend for the staff-holding arm so the hand lands where the staff needs to be gripped.

I'll settle on wrist at (-0.44,1.04,0.17) with forearm length checking out close to 0.24, near enough to the nominal 0.28, so I'll proceed with these coordinates for the hand and move to the left arm.

Setting the staff axis position and fist center relative to the wrist, then working out finger capsules curling around the staff to form a believable grip.

Still working out finger placement...

For a full skeleton I need digit chains: each hand gets five fingers with 2-3 joints apiece, so roughly 15 joints per hand, 30 total, keeping me well within the 160 joint budget. The left hand stays open while the right hand's fingers curl along a gripping path, and I'll write a shared helper function to build both hand structures.

Working out the left arm's shoulder, elbow, and wrist positions with proper bone lengths, then sketching the palm as a box extending downward from the wrist with its own direction vector and length.

Setting up the arm chain from shoulder to elbow to wrist, parented to the chest joint, so the wrist joint naturally becomes the tip that fingers attach to. Shoulder armor like a pauldron would then ride on the shoulder joint at the start of that chain.

For the neck and head, I'm deciding between a chain structure and explicit joints — going with explicit joints: a neck joint parented to the chest aiming upward, then a head joint parented to the neck aiming further up and slightly forward, so the head bone naturally points upward.

I'll simplify by using absolute model coordinates everywhere with a bone reference, rather than fiddling with local axes, and add a jaw joint parented to the head aiming forward for the lower jaw piece. Now I'm sketching the head design itself — a half-human, half-cybernetic face in the style of an Overwatch support hero, blending Mercy, Ana, and Lúcio influences, and starting to think through the head's proportions.

I'm working out the skull shape as a scaled ellipsoid with skin-tone coloring, then adding a metallic faceplate with a glowing teal optic over the cybernetic left side, plus a white-teal hood-helmet with a comms boom and a braided ponytail made from a few simple hair shapes.

For the eyes, I'm planning to use decal textures on the skull surface -- a human eye texture with sclera, iris, and brow on the right side, and a glowing teal ring lens for the cyber eye on the left -- projecting them onto the curved head geometry using the decal placement API.

Now I'm sketching the skull proportions: a scaled sphere for the cranium at a specific center position, with a separate jaw/lower-face shape to give the stylized face its structure.

Checking overlap between the jaw and cranium ellipsoids at their shared y-level to make sure the chin doesn't jut out past the cranium's face plane.

For the mouth, I'm thinking of using a simple decal — a small dark curved line painted onto the jaw surface near y=1.675 to suggest a smile, keeping it simple rather than modeling teeth geometry directly.

For the eyes, I'll follow the proven approach from the toon doc example — placing them on the cranium surface using azimuth/elevation around the sphere's center, with roughly ±24° azimuth and calculating elevation so the eye height lands at y≈1.72 given the sphere center at (0,1.735,0.03).

Now I'm working out eye placement angles: with eyes at x=±0.04 and radius 0.085, azimuth comes to about 28°, mirrored for left/right. I'm sketching the human eye as an SVG with sclera, iris, pupil, highlight, and lash details sized to fit the face, while the cyber eye uses a dark socket with a glowing teal ring — applying glow to the decal part since it carries texture.

I'm figuring out how to shape the cyborg faceplate on the left cheek and temple, considering partial sphere geometry versus an extruded outline, but worried about single-sided rendering issues with partial spheres, so leaning toward extruding a drawn eye-plate outline instead.

Actually, a better approach: use a torus ring as a monocle around the left eye, oriented along the surface normal, plus a stuck-on box for the temple plate and a separate cheek vent plate, giving the cyborg half-face a layered mechanical look.

I'm adding a circuit-line decal across the left cheek with a transparent background for extra detail. For the ears, I'm making the left one a comms earpiece disc with teal accents and antenna, keeping the right as a natural skin ellipsoid. For hair, I'm shaping a partial sphere cap restricted to the crown area so it doesn't cover the face, going with a dark auburn undercut style.

Working out the tilt math for that hair cap now—rotating it slightly around the X axis so the hairline sits naturally above the forehead rather than straight down. Figuring out the rotation isn't zero or in extremely rare edge case and needs to be negative to tip the pole backward and raise the front edge correctly.

At the back the edge dips down to about y=1.69, giving lower nape hair. For styling I'll add a swept-back fringe with a few extruded hair tuft blades, plus a short ponytail curving down from the back of the head, tied off with a white ring.

I'm rigging the ponytail as a sweep along curved points attached to the head bone, and setting up an auburn hair color with lighter highlights using a custom shading function that mixes tones based on surface normal direction to simulate top-lit illumination.

For the armor, I want that clean Overwatch-style baked ambient shading plus scribed panel lines, so I'm considering adding decal details to the chest plate—avoiding anything resembling actual franchise logos or emblems, so I'll design my own generic badge motif like a plus-in-hex symbol instead of anything caduceus-like.

Now I'm defining the torso geometry: setting the center line, waist and chest proportions, and writing a piecewise-linear helper function to interpolate the torso radius along the spine chain, plus the under-suit coloring and chest plate placement for the armor.

Actually simpler to split the cuirass into a front chest plate, offsetting its loft stations forward along z, rather than trying to force a single asymmetric shell.

I'm aiming for a build with roughly 250-350 parts totaling around 40k triangles, which means writing several hundred lines of TypeScript carefully using only well-understood primitive APIs since I can't compile it to check.

I'm sketching a helper function for placing boxes relative to bones with position, rotation, and color, while noting that basic box geometry won't give the beveled edges Overwatch armor typically has, so I'll need another approach to fake those bevels.

Since no tool results will come back, I should just commit to writing the module directly. I'll skip RoundedBoxGeometry and instead use extrude with bevel parameters to create beveled armor plates, which should give a nice outlined slab look without extra dependencies.

Now I'm working out the orientation convention for the extrude plates — figuring out which axis is "x" and "y" relative to the viewer's perspective so the armor faces forward correctly, since the model's right/left needs to map properly to world coordinates.

Working out the cross products for left and right side plates, so x=[0,0,-1] faces +X (left view) and x=[0,0,1] faces -X (right view), confirming the sign convention s=+1 for left.

For the plate outlines, I'm opting for chamfered-corner rectangles instead of rounded corners with smoothing, since smoothing can throw errors when cuts cross other edges — chamfered octagon-style outlines give crisp bevelled corners without needing smoothing at all.

Now I'm defining the color palette: whites, teal accents, and graph grays for the overall layout.

Adding white for highlights, plus a teal glow plate on the chest. Now I'm starting the skeleton builder code, setting up the hips joint as the root with a spine role.

Building the spine chain...

Then I'm working out the vertical proportions: neck from 1.5 to 1.62, head center around 1.74, chin at 1.64, head top near 1.835, and with hair the total height lands around 1.85-1.9, which is roughly in line with typical Overwatch character scale.

I'm defining the neck geometry as a rigid rod attached to the neck bone, then adding a lathe-generated collar ring to give that Overwatch-hoodie look around the neckline.

Now I'm placing the hip sockets and computing the leg geometry — figuring out ankle and boot positions, then solving the leg bend using the triangle distance formula between hip, knee, and ankle to get a slight knee displacement since the total leg length slightly exceeds the hip-to-ankle distance.

I'm structuring the limb-building function signature, then writing out the chain calls for the leg joints (hip, knee, ankle) with parenting to the hips, followed by adding a toe joint parented to the ankle, working through how to reference the chain's tip joint correctly with type assertions.

I'm adjusting leg sweep radii to avoid thigh overlap at the pelvis and starting to plan the leg armor pieces, beginning with a thigh guard.

For the thigh plate, I'm computing points along the hip-to-knee axis and offsetting forward slightly, since the knee sits ahead of the hip. I'll use a lerp helper to find a point partway down the thigh, then build a frustum box offset toward the front, or alternatively just sweep a larger-radius ngon tube segment over part of the leg as armor coverage.

Tightening the radius slightly avoids clipping. For the thigh armor, I'm thinking of a dark undersuit sleeve with a lighter plate on the front, like typical Overwatch-style pants, rather than a full-circle wrap.

Computing leg direction vectors to position the extruded plates correctly along the tilted thigh and shin...

I'm designing a generic limb plate helper that takes a bone's endpoints and generates a chamfered rectangular outline, oriented so the y-axis follows the limb direction and x stays frontal—this works cleanly for legs, though arms angled in x may need a different basis since the axes aren't strictly perpendicular.

For arms I'll orthonormalize manually: computing the up vector along the limb, deriving a frontal x-axis by projecting out the up component from a world-x reference, then taking their cross product to get the outward thickness direction for placing the plate.

I'm generalizing this into a `panel` helper that takes a facing direction and an up vector, orthogonalizes them, and derives the perpendicular axis so the plate orients correctly regardless of limb angle.

Now I need to settle the typing for color input, deciding between a plain string, a `Paint` instance, or a shared `ColorInput` type imported from the paint module so all panel calls stay consistent.

With a coordinate helper in place, I'm sketching out the body parts list, starting with the pelvis as a swept vertical tube at the hips with elliptical cross-section, plus a graphite belt piece layered on top.

Since lathe geometry is circular and the torso cross-section is elliptical, I'm switching to a closed sweep along a ring of points to get the right belt shape at the hips, along with utility pouches, a teal buckle plate, and white side skirt panels on the hip bone.

Still working out the sweep cross-section dimensions...

To avoid ambiguity I'll explicitly pass an up vector of [0,1,0] to the ring sweeps. For the torso, I'll sweep the spine chain with radius for the graphite undersuit, then move on to the white arm.

For the chest shell I'll sweep a slightly larger radius along the same spine chain segment (t=0.45 to 0.97) in white, using flat caps to close the ends, reusing the torso's radius-by-t values with a small margin added.

I want it to form a full cuirass over the dark undersuit, leaving the waist and side vents visible below, and I'm considering adding a central sternum plate with a teal core light at the chest front.

I'm computing the decal placement for panel-line texture on the chest shell, positioning it near the surface at the correct height based on the torso's sweep profile. I also want to add a medic-style backpack on the back — a bulky white medical pack with teal accents.

I'm planning the backpack geometry: a chunky plate pair for the pack body, two lathe-built canisters with glowing teal windows, plus vents and hose sweeps connecting to the shoulders or a hip holster for a cable detail, while skipping a drone attachment to keep it simpler.

The left wrist gets a gauntlet with a glowing holographic display plane, and I'm considering a small hovering "healing nanite sphere" above the open palm, though the arm's lowered pose means the hand faces inward rather than up. For the right hand, I'm sizing a tall staff (~1.7 units) so its base touches the floor near the character's foot, with a graphite-and-white segmented shaft and a lathe-built ring cradle at the top holding a glowing teal crystal.

I'll attach the staff rigidly to the wrist bone via a dedicated joint, keeping its role unspecified, and size the shaft to run from the ground up to about 1.52m with the emitter head extending to roughly 1.85m so the overall figure height stays proportional to the hero's.

Now I'm detailing the staff geometry itself: a conical foot grounded at the floor, a white tube shaft with graphite grip wraps and teal accent rings, a glowing inset strip along the front, and a head assembly with a lower collar and curved prongs cradling a small glowing icosahedron crystal.

I'm adding a rotated halo torus around the crystal and two white-and-teal wing fins flanking the head, deciding to skip hanging pennants or charms to keep it clean. Now I'm working out how the right hand grips the staff, positioning the palm behind the shaft so the fingers can wrap forward around it.

Still placing the fist and fingers...

Simplifying this: I'll treat the fingers as wrapping roughly 260° around the staff's axis, starting from the back side and curling clockwise around the outer edge toward the front, then in toward the inner side.

Tracing the angle sweep around the circle: back-outer to front to inner, picking four sample angles to define three finger-chain segments, trying to land the fingertip on the inner-front side.

Adjusting the radius slightly to 0.034 so the chord dips don't intersect the staff too much, and starting to compute the first joint position where the finger connects to the palm.

Now I'm sketching out the thumb as a separate short chain of two spans, positioning it on top near the fingers and pressing diagonally across them with points placed slightly forward and upward from the palm base.

I'm planning the staff to be a child of the wrist joint so it moves naturally with the arm, and deciding to skip nail details but keep a dark glove cuff. For the design, I'm settling on a half-cyborg look: the right arm organic with graphite gloves and subtle teal accents, while the left arm is the robotic half, rendered in metallic grey-silver with exposed hydraulic joints and glowing teal lines to sell the cybernetic contrast.

I'm also deciding to limit the cyber elements to the left arm, eye, and jaw, keeping the legs mostly symmetrical except for a left knee with a cyber knee-cap and teal ring detail for visual interest without overcomplicating things. Now I'm working out the sweep radius keyframes for the arm's sleeve geometry across the shoulder-elbow-wrist chain.

For the left cyber forearm, I'm switching from per-segment colors to a function-based radius approach so I can keep the sweep piecewise-smooth across the whole arm length using a single interpolation function rather than splitting into separate sweeps with mismatched parameterization.

Now I'm detailing the cyber arm components: a graphite elbow joint with a teal ring, thin piston rods along the forearm, white panel plates, glowing teal seam strips, a wrist gauntlet screen, and a metallic grey hand, while the right arm gets a white pauldron sleeve with a graphite glove. I'm also sizing up big hero-style shoulder pauldrons as scaled spheres positioned at each side.

Still refining shoulder geometry... I'm also mapping out the rest of the silhouette: a graphite neck rod, a high white collar with teal trim, head components, and a chest shell with a glowing teal core.

These tasset panels will clip slightly with legs during posing, which I'll accept. Now I'm moving to the backpack, attaching it to the chest bone and figuring out the facing direction for the main panel so it orients correctly on the back.

Thinking through the backpack shape more, I'm sketching a chunky frustum-box form for the top section, then deciding to switch to a beveled rounded-rect panel instead for a cleaner Overwatch-style slab look on the torso back.

I'm working out the gap between the backpack and torso shell, adding a dark mount plate to bridge them, then adding flanking canisters with glowing teal windows, slatted vents on top, and a thin antenna with a glowing tip.

Now I'm routing hoses from the canisters toward the shoulder and hip using curved path points, and planning a decal panel on the back slab with cross-glyph markings and stripe lines, figuring out the projection direction for the decal so it reads correctly from behind.

For the chest texture SVG, I'm sketching panel lines in a V-shape pattern using dark graphite strokes, a teal stripe accent, and a small hex badge, all over a transparent background so the underlying paint color shows through.

Adding the chevron accent and planning the central hex core as a glowing six-sided cylinder oriented along the Z axis at the sternum.

Since the shell is skinned over the spine chain, I should pin the stick to the chest bone explicitly to keep it rigid rather than deform with the sweep. I'll also use hits to place decals via `b.decal`, and guard against the surface query returning null by asserting non-null on the hit result.

Now I'm planning out the texture decals — eye variants, mouth, cheek circuitry, wrist screen, leg panel lines, boot stripes, staff glyph — and starting to write the SVG markup for the human eye shape with its outline and fill colors.

Writing SVG eye markup...

Checking the Bezier curve math to confirm the eye shape spans roughly y=11 to y=31, keeping it within the viewBox bounds.

Now I'm deciding on iris colors — using a warm amber-brown for the human eye and designing the cyber eye as a dark socket with teal ring segments and a bright glowing core.

Writing SVG code...

Now I'm thinking about how the cyber eye decal sits on the cranium at that angle, with a surrounding faceplate framing it.

I'm checking that the surrounding eye ring geometry doesn't clip with the decal and that the radii work out properly. Then I'm positioning a circuit decal on the temple/cheek area with teal glowing lines on a transparent background, making sure the orientation and sizing align with the surface normal, before moving on to placing a decal for the mouth on the jaw bone.

Now I'm working out the mouth placement on the jaw mesh, calculating the elevation angle from the ellipsoid radii so the seam lines up correctly, then sketching a small smile shape with a stroke path and a lighter lower lip ellipse for the mouth decal. I'm also double-checking how the cranium and jaw curvature meet at the seam so the mouth sits naturally at that boundary.

Checking the jaw front position at its top (y=1.668) against the face: it comes out to 0.1065 versus jaw's 0.111, so the chin region sits just slightly ahead, which looks right. The mouth line at y≈1.676 falls between the jaw top (y 1.704) and this level, so the proportions seem to line up correctly.

I'm now orienting the jaw bone to rotate forward from its joint, and placing the eyes on the face ellipsoid using angular offsets rather than raw coordinates, approximating where they'd intersect the curved surface.

Checking overall head height against total body height (~1.9m), the proportions come out close to realistic but maybe slightly small for a heroic stylized look, so I'm considering a uniform head scale factor of around 1.1 rather than redefining every part individually, though I'll set that decision aside for now.

I'm sizing up hands, feet, and shoulders bigger for that stylized Overwatch look, then adding facial details — nose, cheeks, mouth, and ears, with the right ear simple and the left styled as a cybernetic disc piece. Building the facial geometry...

Checking the brow placement, the surface curves back so I'll need a two-segment rod to follow the face contour properly at the outer edge.

For the left side I'm thinking of a metal cyber brow plate—an angular graphite/teal piece as a contrast accent. Then I need to size the hair cap so it fully covers the cranium shape.

Good, forehead stays visible between brows and hairline. Now I'm adding hair strand geometry—sweeping blade shapes back from the hairline over the crown toward the back, using curved sweeps with tapered radii and highlight coloring to give the hair some texture.

I'll use spike cones rooted at surface hit points, angled backward-up to sweep like spiky anime hair strands, arranging multiple rows across varying elevations and azimuths with small cone dimensions for a layered spiky look.

A ponytail sweeping from the back of the cap down behind the neck, tapering in radius and tied with a small torus hair-tie, ending above the backpack top so they don't overlap. I'm also adding a sideburn tuft near the cheek for bangs detail.

Now I'm turning to the cyberized side of the face: a jaw plate and cheek plate made from small flat boxes seated against the surface normal at the hit point, oriented to face outward with simple panel geometry. I'm starting to lay out the actual build script, importing the builder utilities, skeleton joint types, math helpers like lerp, and the IK/path functions (limb, catmull, polyline, arc) I'll need to construct each body section in order.

I'm also pulling in the paint system—mix, paint, smoothstep—and defining a shading helper that blends a highlight and shadow color based on surface normal direction, which I'll use for the white armor plating with a subtle darker tone near the bottom for a weathered look.

I'm sketching out the overall module structure: exporting metadata for the build, defining color constants, and writing a main build function that creates the skeleton builder and returns the root. I'm also setting up small utility functions—a vector constructor, a piecewise linear interpolator, and a rounded-rectangle outline generator for shaping body parts.

I'm defining a panel helper that computes orientation vectors (facing, up, and the derived side axis) from a bone's position to extrude a flat shape with thickness and bevel, passing the color and bone reference into the builder's extrude call, and confirming the direction types accept plain vectors directly.

Now I'm starting to build the full skeleton hierarchy for the figure, defining joints for the hips and a spine chain built from a smooth curve through several points, then extracting the chest joint from that chain to use as a parent for upper body parts.

I'm thinking about role conflicts between the root hip joint and the spine chain's first segment, deciding to leave the role unset on the root joint to keep things unambiguous. From there I'm setting up the neck, head, and jaw joints with aim targets pointing roughly forward and upward, then moving on to mirror the arm construction for both sides of the body.

For the arms, I'm working out shoulder, elbow, and wrist coordinates for left and right sides separately, checking that the forearm direction for the right arm points plausibly forward. Then I'm building a generic `arm(s)` function that constructs a named chain (e.g. "armL"/"armR") from shoulder to elbow to wrist, parented to the chest, confirming that point arrays work fine as chain input.

Next I'm thinking through how to sweep radius along the arm chain with varying thickness, applying graphite sleeve coloring to the upper arm and differentiating forearm materials (glove sleeve on the right, metal on the left). I'm also planning white armor panels—shoulder pauldron, upper arm guard, and forearm bracers—oriented to face outward based on the arm's natural outward tilt, computing axis vectors from shoulder to elbow to determine that outward-facing direction.

Writing limb frame helpers...

Still defining leg chains...

Still working out leg armor geometry...

Still positioning the knee ring geometry...

Adding shin guard panel geometry...

Mapping out the boot silhouette as a profile polygon, tracing heel to toe to the shin, so I can extrude it into a chunky boot shape.

Mapping out the boot outline points going around counter-clockwise from heel to toe to top, checking that the polygon stays simple without self-intersecting.

For the sole, I'm sketching a thin strip slightly larger than the boot bottom, about 0.03 high, that would sit flush with the boot's base—since both bottoms are at y=0, their faces are coplanar there but that's hidden from view so z-fighting isn't a visual concern.

Now I'm working out the toe cap: a graphite panel slightly larger than the boot silhouette so it protrudes just a bit (around 0.004 on each side), with the same outline shape as the boot but offset in thickness and bevel to read as a distinct cap rather than clipping flush.

I decide the toe cap geometry should attach to the toe bone rather than the ankle, so it moves naturally with the foot's rigid weighting. I'm also planning additional boot details — thin glowing teal straps across the instep, a graphite velcro strap near the shin top, a small buckle, and maybe a few rivets.

Moving on to the hips, I'm sketching out the pelvis structure: a tube shape with belt rings, pouches, hip plates, groin coverage, and tabard-style skirt panels, starting with a belt ring sweep positioned at the hip height using an elliptical cross-section sized to match the pelvis taper into the torso.

Working out the belt radius sizing so it sits just outside the torso and pelvis curves at that height, then building a closed ring of points for a smooth sweep. I'm defining the belt as a boxed sweep around that ring with specific radial and vertical half-extents, oriented so its flat face stays upright. Then I add a front buckle plate panel, plus side pouches extending outward from the belt, including a larger medkit-style pouch on one hip, possibly marked with a white cross.

I'm now planning a decal approach for markings like a teal plus sign, using a textured plane part placed and oriented against a bone, and writing a reusable helper function for placing these flat decal planes with configurable size, direction, and texture. I'm also positioning rounded hip armor plates on the outer sides of the pelvis, calculating their offset so they clear the leg and pelvis radii without overlapping awkwardly.

I'm shaping the front and back tabard flaps as trapezoid panels hanging below the belt, checking their depth offset against the pelvis tube radius to avoid clipping, and planning a thin teal stripe down the center of each flap before sweeping the pelvis tube shape itself.

Realizing round end caps would make the pelvis dome dip too deep between the legs, so I'm switching to flat caps at the start and bottom of the pelvis sweep to keep the silhouette proportionate.

Checking that the torso's start cap dome stays tucked inside the pelvis radius so the seam stays hidden — the dimensions work out fine there.

For the chest shell, I need to make sure the top cap doesn't accidentally dome upward past y=1.5 into head territory, so flat caps seem safer than round ones for that top edge.

Chest joint placement looks fine as is, with the shell colored plain white and no extra banding. For the waist, I'm thinking the undersuit shows as graphite between the belt and shell start, possibly with teal accent lines or an abs panel decal on the torso.

I'll add that abs decal onto the torso front with grid lines in a lighter graphite plus a teal tick mark, skipping the corset ring detail entirely. The back of the torso will house the backpack mount, and for shoulders I'm placing a scaled white pauldron sphere at the shoulder joint, working out its center position, radii, and rotation so it tilts outward and down correctly for each side.

Now I'm layering a trim plate beneath the pauldron plus a thin teal glow torus around its lower rim, carefully working through the rotation math so the torus lies flat and tilts to match the pauldron's outward angle.

Working through the trig gives dir = [s*0.342, 0.94, 0] for the pauldron's up axis, so I'll use that as the direction vector with axis "z" for the torus and axis "y" for the cylinders.

For the pauldron pieces I'm planning a white dome, a lower rim ring made from a tapered cylinder, a glow torus, and a teal chevron decal applied onto the dome's curved surface near the top. Then I'm adding the outer upper-arm white plate panel between the shoulder and elbow joints.

For the elbow I'm placing a graphite sphere joint with a flattened white guard positioned slightly behind it. The right forearm gets an organic sleeve-and-glove look with tapering radius, white bracer plates, and a graphite cuff, while the left cyber forearm uses grey metal plating with exposed hydraulic pistons as thin silver rods, ring segments, teal accent strips, and a wrist gauntlet with a holo panel.

I'm figuring out the holo screen placement on the left forearm's outer face, as a small glowing textured plane framed by a graphite panel, oriented based on how the arm hangs. Then I'm working out the left hand structure — a palm shape with four fingers and a thumb built as jointed chains, positioning the hand continuing the forearm's direction but curled slightly, with the palm centered at the wrist.

Now I'm determining finger curl and orientation, figuring the hand's width axis runs front-to-back so the index finger sits forward and the pinky toward the back, with the palm facing inward toward the thigh and the thumb positioned near the front-inner side.

Still computing finger joint positions...

Working through the Frenet frame math for the downward-pointing arm tube, I'm figuring out that the binormal ends up aligned with X, meaning that's the axis governing the hand's thickness versus width for a hanging arm orientation.

For the fingers, I'm planning to sweep thin tapered chains along each digit colored metal grey, and considering adding tiny glowing teal spheres at the fingertips for a subtle highlight.

Now I'm setting up the right hand's finger wraps and thumb, adding a small panel plate on the back of the hand, and placing tapered cylinder cuffs aligned along the forearm direction at each wrist. Then I'm moving on to constructing the staff, positioning its vertical axis and attaching it as a child joint off the right wrist.

Writing staff geometry...

Now moving to the staff head: I'm lathing a collar shape at y=1.5 with a curved profile for the white shaded base, then adding four curved prongs rising from the collar to cradle the crystal.

Placing the four prongs diagonally at 45°, 135°, 225°, 315°, then shaping the crystal as a stretched icosahedron with teal glow and flat shading, plus adding a thin horizontal halo ring around it.

Still writing geometry parameters...

Mirroring the fin shape for the opposite side and positioning it with the extrude call...

Now I'm thinking about additional details: a teal glow dot at the staff tip, thin glow panels on the wings, a small hex medal on the collar front, and a hanging teal cloth strip from the collar for a tassel effect.

I'm also considering a beam emitter nozzle on the staff for the healing effect, then moving on to backpack hose details and head items — specifically a boom mic curving from the left earcup down to near the mouth, since the right side already has a cyber ear piece.

For the face, I'm setting up a face surface helper to project hit points onto an ellipsoid centered around the character's cheek area, then placing a small cheek plate box there oriented so its thin dimension sinks into the skin along the surface normal.

Next I'm planning a brow plate sweep piece, a temple plate on the cranium with a glowing teal seam, and a cyber eye ring using a torus placed via a frame hit on the head bone.

Checking that b.surface accepts any target including a Surface works for the decal call. I'm sizing the eye decals at .05 width with centers spaced .08 apart, and calculating the hit elevation (6°) to land the eye position around y≈1.724.
